problem: Most AI tools give you pieces: a component, a plugin, a bot.
None of them is a way of working your team builds. And what the AI learns gets lost, in one chat, on one laptop.
turn: {name} is a toolbox your team builds as it needs, reusing the tools you already have.
It starts small, and grows into how your team already works.
map: Your tech lead maps how the team works: the systems, the steps, and the checks.
join: Then the whole team works through it, every day.
Each piece of work teaches the developer and the agent at the same time.
steer: Nothing starts until you say yes.
And it is not done until an independent check passes.
memory: Every lesson goes into one shared place, in plain files.
One file becomes topics, then a playbook for each system.
Teach it a new skill, and it shows you more of your system.
compounds: The more people use it, the more it knows: more playbooks, more fixes.
Anything spotted on the way is recorded and sorted later. Urgent items go to a person straight away.
history: Version control kept your code. This keeps the why: the decisions, the goals, and how it was tested.
How did we do this a year ago? It's written down.
When someone leaves, their knowledge stays. Someone new starts from it.
results: Here is a real team's story. They started small. Seven weeks later:
playbooks covered nearly 9 in 10 pieces of the agent's work, up from 6 in 10.
The backlog of pending software updates shrank by 86%.
And 57% of work found something on the way. 1 in 6 of those findings is already a fix or planned work.
It got faster too. Half of finished work needed no one to type a word, and the agent did 78% of it.
end: After a while, it runs itself: the memory, the plans and the checks all grow in one place.
It's all yours. Stop any time, and keep everything.
